question.text: Why does a Cat III AIF's convertible arbitrage strategy incur a 'borrowing fee' for short equity positions?

answer.text: The fund borrows shares from a securities lender (typically via SLB or prime broker) and pays a borrow fee; dividends during the short period are also forgone/paid to the lender.
SEBI levies a short-sale tax on Cat III AIFs.
It is a penalty for exceeding 2x leverage.
It is a fee paid to the Acquirer in a merger deal.

explanation.text: The Logic: Short-selling in India requires borrowing shares via SLB or prime broker; the fund pays a borrow fee (typically 50-500 bps p.a. depending on stock tightness) plus forgoes/pays dividends accrued during the short. Section 10.1.3 computes this in Example 10.6. The Trap: A invents a tax. C mis-frames the fee as a penalty. D is irrelevant. Cross-Exam Context: VIII (Derivatives) covers SLB mechanics. XIX-C same. Manager's Pro-Tip: Hard-to-borrow stocks can see borrow fees spike 20-30% overnight (squeeze risk). Before entering a merger-arb short, get a term-locked borrow quote (30-day minimum) from the prime broker so fee shock doesn't wreck the spread math.
